description: Andrew Kim brings AI research and USACO Platinum experience. Edison Yang has NASA SEES and astrophysics research experience. Neel Marripalapu brings award-winning work in machine learning and robotics. Luke Wu has quantitative development and competitive programming experience. Akshaj Agadi researches AI reliability and placed second in HouseEdge at TAMU Datathon. Together, we built EarthWitness to make NASA data easier to understand.
summary:
EarthWitness is a web application designed to help people verify environmental claims about our changing planet using NASA Earth science data. Users can enter a claim, such as "The Sahel is getting drier," and EarthWitness will identify the relevant NASA datasets, geographic region, and time period to investigate the claim. The application then analyzes the available records and presents a more precise, evidence-based conclusion supported by interactive graphs, maps, and uncertainty estimates.

Additionally, users can select any location on Earth to explore how its temperature, water, vegetation, ice, and atmospheric conditions have changed over time, as well as identify potential relationships between these environmental trends.

EarthWitness addresses NASA's "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge by guiding users through the process of investigating environmental questions, identifying appropriate datasets, analyzing trends, and evaluating the strength of the supporting evidence. We developed EarthWitness for students, educators, and anyone interested in understanding environmental change. Our goal is to make NASA's extensive collection of Earth science data more accessible and help users draw meaningful, scientifically supported conclusions about how our planet is changing.
details:
The Problem

“The Sahel is getting drier.” It’s a claim that seems reasonable at first glance, especially given the region’s long history of drought. But when we examined NASA’s Earth observation data, we discovered that the reality was more complicated. Rainfall, soil moisture, and terrestrial water storage had all increased over their respective observation periods. This raised a larger question: how many environmental claims do we accept without ever examining the data behind them?

Environmental claims like this appear constantly in news headlines and social media, yet most people have no straightforward way to investigate them. NASA provides decades of publicly available Earth observation data, but interpreting these records often requires specialized knowledge and experience working with scientific datasets. Even a seemingly simple question can involve comparing measurements from different sources or accounting for natural fluctuations that make long-term trends difficult to identify.

We wanted to make it possible for anyone to investigate these questions without needing a background in climate science or programming.

Our Solution: EarthWitness

We developed EarthWitness, an interactive web application that allows users to investigate environmental claims using NASA Earth science data. Our goal was to make scientific investigation accessible to anyone, beginning with a question or statement written in everyday language.

When a user enters a claim, EarthWitness identifies which environmental measurements are relevant and determines the geographic area and time period being discussed. It then analyzes the corresponding NASA records to evaluate whether the evidence supports the claim. Based on the results, the application produces a more precise version of the original statement, accompanied by interactive visualizations and statistical evidence. Users can click on individual parts of the revised statement to examine the measurements behind each conclusion.

For example, when investigating "The Sahel is getting drier," EarthWitness examines different interpretations of the word "drier" and compares their corresponding measurements. The application explains its findings and allows users to explore the geographic trends and statistical significance behind each conclusion.

EarthWitness can also investigate more complex environmental statements, including historical temperature records and comparisons between geographic regions. Users can test claims such as "Global warming stopped in 1998" or "The Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the world" and examine how the available measurements support or contradict them.

Exploring Earth as an Interconnected System

Beyond checking individual claims, we developed a feature called "Read a Place," which allows users to investigate how different components of the Earth system are changing together.

Users can select a country or geographic region directly from an interactive map. EarthWitness then analyzes 24 environmental measurements covering different aspects of the Earth system, from surface temperature and precipitation to vegetation and atmospheric composition. The application organizes these measurements into yearly visualizations, making it possible to compare long-term environmental changes within the same region.

We also developed an interactive system for investigating relationships between environmental variables. EarthWitness statistically tests whether different measurements change together and displays the relationships it identifies through a network diagram. Users can select individual connections to examine the underlying records and investigate how environmental conditions relate to larger climate processes, including El Niño.

For example, exploring India reveals an interesting combination of increasing atmospheric haze and expanding vegetation alongside declining terrestrial water storage. EarthWitness also searches for regions experiencing contrasting trends. One example is the increase in atmospheric haze over India compared with its decline over central China.

By examining multiple environmental records within the same geographic area, users can develop a more complete understanding of how different parts of the Earth system interact. This also creates opportunities to investigate environmental patterns that may be overlooked when studying individual variables.

Technical Development and Innovation

Developing EarthWitness required integrating environmental data processing with natural language interpretation and interactive statistical analysis.

We assembled datasets from NASA missions and scientific products, including GISTEMP, MERRA-2, GPM, MODIS, CERES, GRACE, OMI, and AIRS. Using Python libraries such as NumPy, SciPy, xarray, and Zarr, we processed these measurements into standardized geographic grids and compact data files suitable for browser-based analysis.

The web application was developed using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, D3.js, and Web Workers. Its architecture allows users to interactively explore environmental measurements and generate statistical results directly in their browsers. Because the core application operates on preprocessed NASA datasets, it can run on static web hosting without requiring user accounts or external API credentials.

A major focus of our development was translating natural language into scientifically testable questions. We designed a claim interpretation system that extracts relevant information from user input and converts it into structured queries. The system recognizes environmental variables and geographic references while also interpreting more complex expressions involving changes over time. These queries are passed to our statistical analysis engine, which evaluates the corresponding NASA records.

We also explored machine learning to improve how EarthWitness interprets environmental language. Using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), we fine-tuned a Qwen language model on custom-generated examples involving environmental measurements and geographic references. We subsequently developed a training pipeline using Qwen3-1.7B to interpret more complex statements and translate them into standardized claims. This approach provides a foundation for expanding EarthWitness's natural language capabilities while keeping the scientific calculations within a dedicated statistical analysis system.

Scientific Validation and Reliability

Scientific reliability was an important consideration throughout development. Environmental measurements naturally fluctuate over time, meaning that an apparent increase or decrease does not necessarily represent a statistically significant trend.

To address this, we implemented statistical methods including the Theil-Sen slope estimator and Mann-Kendall trend testing. Our analysis also incorporates confidence intervals and corrections for temporal autocorrelation, which accounts for the tendency of environmental measurements from nearby years to be related. For geographic trend maps, we apply false-discovery-rate controls to reduce the likelihood of identifying misleading patterns across large numbers of locations.

We evaluated these methods using simulated environmental records and comparisons with established scientific findings. In simulations containing no genuine trends, our statistical tests maintained false-positive rates between 3% and 7%, compared with rates as high as 31% for an uncorrected Mann-Kendall test under the same conditions.

We also tested whether EarthWitness could reproduce previously published scientific results. The application successfully recovered established patterns involving Arctic warming and Greenland ice loss, with estimated values closely matching published measurements. For example, our analysis estimated September Arctic sea ice decline at approximately 11.9% per decade, compared with the published value of 12.1%.

We also evaluated our claim interpretation system on previously unseen environmental statements. These tests included misleading claims and complex sentence structures designed to challenge the application's interpretation. For example, one test presented the claim, "Global temperatures have shot up by 3 degrees Celsius since 1980." The challenge was to recognize that global temperatures had increased while also identifying that the claimed magnitude was exaggerated, with the actual increase closer to 0.9°C. In our most recent blind evaluation of 136 claims, 79% received acceptable initial verdicts, while 3% received confidently incorrect conclusions. These results guided further improvements to the interpretation system, with our evaluation procedures and results documented in our public repository.

Impact and Connection to the NASA Space Apps Challenge

EarthWitness directly addresses the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge by incorporating its five core steps into one accessible workflow. Users can select environmental variables and geographic regions, examine historical time series, and evaluate the statistical significance of observed changes.

We designed EarthWitness with a broad audience in mind. Students can use it to investigate climate-related questions for research projects, while educators can demonstrate how scientists evaluate trends using real NASA measurements. The application can also serve journalists and members of the public who want to verify environmental statements they encounter online.

One of the most valuable educational features is the ability to see how an original claim is revised in response to scientific evidence. Instead of receiving only a verdict, users can examine the underlying analysis and understand why specific parts of a statement were corrected. The interactive format encourages users to question assumptions and explore the available evidence themselves.

NASA has spent decades collecting information about our changing planet, and we believe that information should be accessible to far more people. With EarthWitness, we hope to make scientific investigation something anyone can participate in, whether they are researching a question for school or questioning a headline they saw that morning.

Our goal is to make investigating environmental claims as accessible as the information itself. The next time someone reads that a region is getting drier or that global warming has slowed, we want them to be able to examine NASA's records and understand what the measurements actually show. With EarthWitness, we hope to give more people the confidence and tools to ask their own questions about our changing planet, and the ability to find answers grounded in scientific evidence.
